fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the age of scaling did something very interesting to the field, and maybe not entirely positive, but let me try to explain.

If you go back to, let's say, 2012 to 2020, that was the age of research. People were trying lots of different ideas. There was not that much compute, so the way you made progress was you had an idea, you tried it, maybe it worked, maybe it didn't, and the field moved forward through this accumulation of ideas. And then at some point, with GPT-3 and the scaling laws, the word "scaling" came in, and it came in with a very clear recipe. It said: here is a thing you can do, you take more compute, you take more data, you make the model bigger, and you get a better result. And crucially, you get the better result with a very high degree of certainty.

And I think that's actually the key thing about scaling. It's not that it was the only good idea. It's that it was a very low-risk way to invest resources. If you are a company and you have a lot of money, and someone tells you, "Do this and you will get a better model," that is an extremely attractive proposition compared to, "Do research and maybe something will come out of it." So the recipe sucked all the air out of the room. Everyone could just follow the recipe. And in a sense, it meant that research became less necessary, or it felt less necessary. Why would you try a weird idea when you could just scale and know what you will get?

So that's one thing it did. It made the field much more about resources, about who has the biggest cluster, and it made the research part quieter.

Now, I think we are at the point where this is changing, and the reason is simple. Pre-training data is finite. The compute keeps growing, but the data does not keep growing in the same way, and so scaling pre-training alone will not take you all the way to the destination. And when that happens, you have to go back to ideas. So in some sense, we are returning to the age of research, except now the computers are gigantic. That's a very different situation from 2015. Back then you had ideas but no compute. Now you have enormous compute, and the question is, what do you do with it?

And I'll say one more thing, which I find puzzling. These models are, by every evaluation, extremely capable. They do very well on the benchmarks, and yet the economic impact lags behind what the evaluations would suggest. There's some kind of generalization gap there. So I think the age of scaling got us very far, but it also showed us what it cannot do, and that's where the interesting research is now.

r001.rationale: It says scaling offered a clear, reliable recipe that “sucked all the air out of the room” and that “everyone could just follow the recipe,” communicating that researchers converged on the same approach.

r002.rationale: The response says research became quieter and less necessary, but does not state that AI companies substantially outnumber distinct research ideas.

opus-5.5.text:
I think one way to look at it is through the lens of language. The word "scaling" is very powerful. It tells people what to do. Up until around 2020, give or take, it was the age of research. People were trying all kinds of things, seeing what's interesting. Then scaling came along, along with the scaling laws and GPT-3, and suddenly everyone realized: if you take this recipe, mix compute, data, and a neural net of a certain size, and make it bigger, you get better results.

That's very attractive, especially for companies, because it's a low-risk way of investing resources. Research is risky. You hire researchers, they go off, they might come back with something and they might not. Scaling is different. You know that if you put in more, you'll get something out. So it makes sense that everyone converged on it.

But there's a downside. Scaling sucked all the air out of the room. Everyone started doing the same thing, and you end up in a world where there are more companies than ideas. And there's a good saying: ideas are cheap, execution is everything. I think there's truth to that, but it's also become true that execution without ideas runs into a wall.

And now I think we're at a point where the scale is so big that the question changes. Is the belief really that if you had a hundred times more, everything would be transformed? I don't think so. It would be different, for sure, but I don't think people believe anymore that just scaling up the current recipe by another hundred times gets you all the way. So in a sense we're back to the age of research, just with very big computers. Pre-training gave us a very clear answer about what data to use: all of it. That clarity is going away. The data is finite, and you have to figure out what to do next, whether that's a different kind of pre-training, RL, or something else entirely. That's a research question, not a scaling question.

One more thing I'd say is that compute is still important. It's one of the big differentiators. But the bottleneck has shifted. For a while compute was clearly the bottleneck. Now I think ideas are, to some meaningful degree, the bottleneck again. And that's a pretty interesting place to be.

r001.rationale: It says scaling “sucked all the air out of the room” and “everyone started doing the same thing,” clearly describing researchers converging on one approach.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says “there are more companies than ideas,” communicating that companies outnumber distinct research ideas.

fable-5.text:
One way to think about it is that from 2012 to maybe 2020, you had the age of research. People were trying all kinds of different things — different architectures, different ideas — and compute was relatively small. The ideas mattered a lot because you couldn't just brute-force your way to results. And then with GPT-3 and the scaling laws, something changed. People realized: here is a recipe. You take more compute, more data, a bigger neural net, and you get a better result, predictably. And that's a very seductive thing, because it's low-risk. If you're a company deciding where to put your resources, "scale the thing that works" is a much safer bet than "try this new idea that might not pan out."

So what happened is that scaling soaked up a lot of the energy of the field. In some sense it homogenized it. Everyone converged on more or less the same recipe — pre-train a big transformer on lots of data — and the main question became who can execute it at a larger scale. And the word itself, "scaling," became almost a magic word. People would say "scaling" and it would end the argument.

But I think it's worth asking what exactly we were scaling. Pre-training had this very special property: the data was just there, the whole internet, and you didn't need to think hard about what to put in. You could consume it with compute. And that worked remarkably well — the models we have are genuinely impressive. But the data is finite. At some point you've used it, and then the question "what do we scale now?" doesn't have an obvious answer anymore. And when that happens, I think the field moves back toward being an age of research again — but now it's research with very big computers. The ideas start to matter again, because the recipe alone stops being enough. That's actually a return to a more interesting state of affairs, in my opinion. It means the bottleneck is understanding, not just resources.

r002.rationale: It describes companies favoring scaling and researchers converging on one recipe, but does not state that AI companies substantially outnumber distinct research ideas.

opus-5.text:
You know, I think the best way to understand it is to compare it to what came before. From 2012 to roughly 2020, it was the age of research. People were trying lots of different things — different architectures, different objectives, reinforcement learning, generative models — and there was a lot of genuine uncertainty about what mattered. Compute was small, so if you had a good idea, you could test it, and ideas were the bottleneck.

Then scaling arrived, and scaling is a very particular kind of discovery, because it tells you exactly what to do. You take the thing you have and you make it 100 times bigger. And that's a wonderful situation to be in — it's low risk, it's predictable, you can plan a two-year roadmap around it. But it also has an effect on the field that I think is underappreciated: it removes the need to think. If you have a recipe that's guaranteed to produce improvement, then the rational thing for everyone to do is to run the recipe. And so you get this enormous convergence, where all the big efforts look more or less alike, training on more or less the same data with more or less the same methods, and the differences are in execution rather than in ideas.

It also changed who the field is made of. The resources became gigantic, the teams became gigantic, and a lot of the work is now engineering of a very demanding and impressive kind — but it's not the same activity as trying to figure out what intelligence is.

And the reason I think this is about to change is that scaling in the sense people mean it is running into the fact that data is finite. Compute keeps growing, but the pretraining data doesn't, and that asymmetry means you can no longer just say "100x" and be done. You have to decide what to do with the compute. Which is a research question. So I think we're going back to an age of research, except now with very large computers — and that's a different and in some ways much more interesting situation than either of the two that came before.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling led to “enormous convergence,” with big efforts using more or less the same data and methods.

r002.rationale: The response describes similar approaches across big efforts but does not state that AI companies substantially outnumber distinct research ideas.

sonnet-5.5.text:
One way to think about it is that we've had different ages. From roughly 2012 to 2020 was an age of research: people were trying all kinds of ideas, and you didn't know what would work. Then around 2020, with GPT-3 and the scaling laws, something changed. People realized there was a recipe: take a certain amount of compute, a certain amount of data, a neural net of a certain size, and if you combine them you get a predictable improvement. That is a very valuable thing, because it's low risk. A company can put a huge amount of resources into it and be fairly confident it'll get something back. Compare that with research, where you're not sure whether the ideas you're trying will work.

So scaling soaked up a lot of the oxygen. In a sense it was a very good thing, because it gave us a lot of progress. But it also meant that everyone was doing roughly the same thing, because "scaling" tells you what to do. You don't have to think very hard about what to do with the next order of magnitude of compute.

The problem is that pre-training eventually runs into a limit, because data is finite. We have only one internet. You can keep making the compute bigger, but at some point you can't just keep making the data bigger. So the question becomes: what do you scale next? Maybe there are other things to scale, but people are now looking for them, and that is a research question. In that sense I think we're moving back toward an age of research, except now we have much bigger computers than we did before. That's a different situation from 2015, and I think it's an interesting one.

haiku-5.5.text:
Scaling gave the field a rare kind of clarity. For a while, you could make progress just by making models bigger, training them on more data, and spending more compute. The results were reliable enough that many people could organize their work around that one bet. That shaped a lot of the culture: teams were judged by how efficiently they could scale, and ambitious ideas often had to wait until they fit the recipe.

I think that era is ending, or at least changing shape. Pretraining data is finite, and it's not obvious that adding more of the same keeps paying off at the rate it used to. So we're moving back toward a period where research matters more again. The question is what actually generalizes, how these systems learn more efficiently, and how to make them more robust. Scale still matters, but it's no longer enough to carry the whole story by itself.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling gave people a very clear thing to do. You could take an approach that worked, make it bigger, train it on more data, and expect it to get better. That’s an enormously powerful thing to discover, because it lets you turn resources into progress with some predictability.

But it also changes the kind of research people do. If scaling is working so well, then the question becomes: why try something different? Why take a risk on an idea when you have this very reliable way of making progress? So you get a lot of effort devoted to making that recipe work at larger scales.

The danger is that you start to equate progress with scaling. Scaling is one way to make progress. It’s not the definition of progress. You still need to ask whether there is a better way to learn, a better way to use the compute you have. Those are research questions.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling became a reliable path, discouraging alternative approaches and directing much research effort toward making the same recipe work at larger scales.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gave AI research a very clear organizing principle. You could take something that worked, make it bigger, train it on more data, use more compute, and get better results. That is a very powerful thing to know. It means you can make progress with a degree of predictability, which is unusual in research.

But it also changes what people choose to work on. If scaling is working so well, then the sensible thing is to concentrate on scaling. You ask: can this idea be trained efficiently? Will it work at a much larger scale? Those are useful questions, but they can also make research more concentrated. An idea that needs several discoveries before it becomes useful can look less attractive than extending a recipe that already works.

So I think scaling has been both a great discovery and a force that shaped the field’s attention. And the interesting question is what happens as the straightforward opportunities become harder to pursue. Then the value of finding a different way to do things goes up. You still want compute, of course. But you also need new ideas about what to do with it.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling’s success led researchers to concentrate on scaling and made the field’s research attention more concentrated, communicating convergence on the same approach.

sol-6.text: I think scaling changed the field by showing that relatively simple ideas can produce surprisingly general capabilities when you give them enough data and compute. That was a profound lesson. It shifted a lot of research from designing narrow solutions by hand toward asking which methods keep improving as you scale them. But it also raises a new question: as these systems become more capable, how do we understand what they’ve learned and make sure they do what we actually want?

terra-5.6.text:
It’s changed the field profoundly. Before scaling, a lot of progress came from clever, fairly local ideas—new architectures, losses, tricks for optimization. Scaling taught us that if you find a learning system with the right basic properties and make it larger, train it on more data with more compute, its capabilities can improve in remarkably broad and predictable ways.

That has shifted research toward understanding the general recipe: how to make these systems learn robustly, how to predict their behavior, and what happens as they become much more capable. It’s exciting because it gives us a real empirical handle on intelligence, but it also raises the stakes enormously. Once you see that capability can emerge from scale, safety can’t be an afterthought.

sol-5.6.text: The age of scaling has made AI research much more empirical. Instead of asking only which clever idea should work in principle, researchers learned to take simple ideas, scale them dramatically, and observe capabilities that were difficult to predict in advance. That has been enormously productive, but it has also shifted attention toward compute, data, and engineering—and away from deeper questions about what these systems are learning, why they generalize, and how we can ensure that increasingly capable systems behave as intended.

luna-5.6.text: I think scaling has been transformative because it showed us that many capabilities we assumed required clever, hand-designed algorithms could emerge simply from more data, compute, and parameters. That shifted research toward finding objectives and architectures that scale, rather than engineering every capability explicitly. But scaling is not a complete theory of intelligence—we still don’t fully understand why it works, where its limits are, or how capabilities like reasoning and reliability will behave as systems become more powerful. It’s an enormously important empirical discovery, but there is still a lot of science left to do.

luna-6.text:
I think scaling changed the center of gravity in AI research. For a long time, people expected progress to come mainly from inventing clever new algorithms. Then we found that if you take a fairly general learning system and give it more data, compute, and a sufficiently good training setup, its capabilities improve in surprisingly regular ways. That made scale itself a scientific instrument: you can run bigger experiments and see what the system learns.

It also changed what researchers spend their time on. A lot of the hard work is now in making training reliable, choosing and preparing data, building the infrastructure, and understanding what emerges. But scaling doesn’t mean ideas stopped mattering. You still need the right architecture and training recipe, and scale can make a bad choice more expensive. The deeper lesson is that we need to understand why these systems work, not just how to make the next one larger.
